result: Compound heterozygous mutations in CFAP52 (c.203G>T and c.1128G>A) were identified in a Chinese infertile patient through whole-exome sequencing. These variants are extremely rare in population databases, highly conserved across species, and segregate recessively with the infertility phenotype in the family.
evaluation: Claims C18-C20 and C98-C105 provide comprehensive genetic evidence including WES identification, Sanger sequencing validation, segregation analysis, allele frequency data, conservation analysis, and computational predictions. The data consistently support the identification and characterization of these CFAP52 variants.

result: Both CFAP52 mutations result in complete loss of protein expression. The c.1128G>A nonsense mutation abolishes protein expression, while the c.203G>T variant causes exon 2 deletion leading to a frameshift and loss of protein. CFAP52 protein was undetectable in patient spermatozoa.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 and C26 are supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches including western blotting of transfected cells, minigene splicing assays, Sanger sequencing of transcripts, and immunofluorescence of patient spermatozoa. The data consistently demonstrate complete loss of CFAP52 protein.

result: The CFAP52-mutant patient exhibits severe asthenoteratozoospermia with reduced sperm motility (6.0% A+B), abnormal morphology (99.5% defective), multiple morphological abnormalities of flagella (MMAF), and high sperm decapitation rate (34.0%).
evaluation: Claims C12-C14 and C93-C97 are supported by comprehensive semen analysis data presented in Table 1 and microscopy images in Figure 1. The quantitative parameters and morphological observations consistently demonstrate severe sperm defects.

result: Ultrastructural analysis of patient spermatozoa revealed defects in the head-tail connecting piece (incomplete/invisible proximal centrioles, defective segmented columns) and flagellar axoneme abnormalities (disorganized/missing central pairs, disordered outer dense fibers and doublet microtubules).
evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1C. The TEM images provide direct visualization of the ultrastructural defects at the connecting piece and flagellar axoneme level.

result: Cfap52-knockout mice generated by CRISPR/Cas9 completely lack CFAP52 protein, develop hydrocephalus with sparse ependymal cilia and disrupted axonemal structures, but show normal tracheal cilia. Male Cfap52-KO mice are completely sterile.
evaluation: Claims C29-C35 are supported by comprehensive characterization including genotyping, western blotting (Figure 4C), SEM/TEM analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and fertility testing (Figure 4D-E). The data consistently demonstrate successful knockout and resulting phenotypes.

result: Cfap52-KO mice produce reduced numbers of spermatozoa with poor motility. Approximately 40% show decapitation, 25% have abnormal head-tail connections, and 30% exhibit deformed flagella.
evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by quantitative sperm analysis (Figure 4F-G) and Papanicolaou staining with morphological quantification (Figure 4H-I). The data provide both quantitative measurements and morphological characterization of sperm defects.

result: Cfap52-KO spermatids show defective connecting piece formation including enlarged gaps between nuclear envelope and axoneme, ectopically localized mitochondria and vacuoles, and misaligned flagella. The percentage of spermatids with ultrastructural defects is significantly greater than in WT mice.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by detailed TEM analysis (Figure 5A) and statistical quantification (Figure 5B-C). The ultrastructural observations are systematically categorized and quantified, providing strong evidence for connecting piece defects.

result: Cfap52-KO spermatozoa exhibit severe flagellar axoneme defects throughout the flagellum including disordered axoneme and accessory structures in the midpiece, partial loss of axoneme and ODFs in the principal piece, and absent/disordered central pairs and doublet microtubules in the end piece.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by comprehensive TEM analysis of flagellar cross-sections (Figure 5D) with statistical quantification (Figure 5E). The data systematically document axonemal defects across all flagellar regions.

result: CFAP52 interacts with SPATA6 and is essential for its stability. SPATA6 expression is significantly reduced in Cfap52-KO testis and barely detectable in patient spermatozoa. CFAP52 slows SPATA6 degradation in cycloheximide chase assays.
evaluation: Claims C49-C50, C53-C54, and C66 are supported by multiple complementary approaches including western blotting (Figure 6A), immunofluorescence (Figure 6B), co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 6C-D), and protein stability assays (Figure 6E-F). The data consistently demonstrate CFAP52-SPATA6 interaction and regulation.

result: Expression of microtubule inner proteins (CFAP45, ENKUR) and radial spoke proteins (RSPH3, RSPH9) is significantly reduced in Cfap52-KO sperm and nearly absent in the CFAP52-mutant patient's sperm flagella.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 and C67-C68 are supported by western blotting analysis (Figure 7A) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 7B). The data demonstrate consistent reduction of specific axonemal protein components in both mouse and human CFAP52 deficiency.

result: CFAP52 interacts with multiple axonemal components including MIPs (CFAP20, PACRG), radial spokes (RSPH1, RSPH3), and outer dynein arm components (DNAI2, ODAD1, ODAD3), but not with inner dynein arm, dynein regulatory complex, or central apparatus components.
evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by systematic co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The data demonstrate selective protein-protein interactions, though the physiological relevance of interactions identified in heterologous cells requires validation.

result: Protein levels of outer dynein arms (DNAI1, DNAI2), inner dynein arms (DNAH7, DNALI1), and dynein regulatory complexes (DRC2, DRC4) are not altered in Cfap52-KO sperm. DNAI1 and DRC3 expression is maintained in patient sperm flagella.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by western blotting (Figure 7A) and immunofluorescence (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). These negative results are important controls demonstrating specificity of the CFAP52 deficiency effects on certain axonemal components.

result: ICSI successfully overcame CFAP52-associated male infertility in the patient, achieving 95.2% fertilization rate, 100% cleavage, and resulting in a healthy live birth. This demonstrates ICSI as a promising treatment for CFAP52-related infertility.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C64, and C69 are supported by detailed ICSI outcome data (Table 3) and successful live birth. However, this represents a single case, and the claim that ICSI is 'promising' (C64) requires validation in additional patients.

result: ICSI using spermatozoa from Cfap52-KO mice successfully produced two-cell embryos and blastocysts with similar efficiency to wild-type controls.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by ICSI experiments in mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 3). The data demonstrate that despite severe morphological defects, Cfap52-KO sperm retain fertilization competence when mechanical barriers are bypassed by ICSI.

result: Cfap52-KO mice show normal testis size, testis/body weight ratio, and serum hormone levels (GnRH, testosterone). Histological examination reveals regular seminiferous epithelium cycles but flagellar formation defects at stage V-VIII.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are supported by morphological measurements, ELISA data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), and histological analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). These data demonstrate that CFAP52 deficiency specifically affects flagellar development without disrupting earlier spermatogenic processes.

result: Cfap52-knockout mice phenocopy the human CFAP52-mutant patient, showing a mixed ASS and MMAF phenotype with failure of connecting piece formation and serious disorder of the 9+2 axoneme structure.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 and C92 are supported by comprehensive morphological and ultrastructural comparisons between mouse and human phenotypes (Figures 1, 4, 5). The mouse model successfully recapitulates the key features of human CFAP52 deficiency.

result: CFAP52 plays a prominent role in sperm development and might be a novel diagnostic target for male infertility with defects of sperm head-tail connection and flagella development.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C65 represent interpretive conclusions. While C70 is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data, C71 and C65 regarding CFAP52 as a 'novel diagnostic target' are speculative and require validation in larger patient cohorts and clinical implementation studies.

result: Prior to this study, no evidence linked CFAP52 mutations to human male infertility. This study identifies compound heterozygous CFAP52 mutations cosegregating with male infertility in a Chinese family.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 accurately represent the novelty of the findings. C90 is supported by literature review, and C91 is supported by WES and segregation analysis. This establishes the first human genetic evidence linking CFAP52 to male infertility.

result: CFAP52 localizes to both HTCA and full-length flagella in normal control spermatozoa. In mice, CFAP52 is highly expressed in testes and localizes to the manchette of spermatids and full-length sperm flagellum. Both CFAP52 and SPATA6 localize to the manchette.
evaluation: Claims C25, C27-C28, and C106 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3F) and citations to prior studies. The localization data are consistent with CFAP52's proposed roles in HTCA and flagellar development.

result: SUN5 staining at the connecting piece is maintained in spermatozoa from the CFAP52-mutant patient, serving as a positive control.
evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). This control demonstrates that not all connecting piece proteins are lost in CFAP52 deficiency, supporting specificity of the SPATA6 reduction.

result: Background context on male infertility, MMAF, ASS, and prior knowledge about CFAP52 from model organisms and human ciliopathies.
evaluation: Claims C1-C11 represent background information supported by appropriate citations. These establish the scientific context for the study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

result: Additional background information on SPATA6 function, CFAP52 interactions, manchette function, HTCA structure, ASS etiology, MMAF etiology, and male infertility classification.
evaluation: Claims C75-C128 represent established knowledge from prior literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings from this study.
